definitions.text: Cranial nerve VI, which emerges at the pontomedullary junction close to the midline, the most medial of the nerves in the bulbopontine groove.

evidence.quote: CN VI, abducens | Pontomedullary junction, near the midline
Cranial nerve VI: abducens originates from the pontomedullary junction, close to the midline

definitions.text: Cranial nerve XI, one of the mixed nerves; its cranial part emerges from the sulcus behind the olive of the medulla, below the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves.

evidence.quote: Lateral, behind the olive | IX, X and XI, the mixed nerves
CN IX, X and the cranial part of XI, from above downwards, from the sulcus behind the olive

definitions.text: The three parameters the lecture uses to characterise the voice: frequency, in Hertz, depending on the vibration speed of the vocal folds; intensity, in dB, depending on the force of pulmonary expiration; and pitch, depending on vocal fold accommodation and especially the shape of the supralaryngeal cavities.

evidence.quote: The voice is characterised by three acoustic parameters: frequency, in Hertz, depending on the vibration speed of the vocal folds
The voice is characterized by 3 acoustic parameters

definitions.text: The association of a peripheral cranial nerve palsy on one side with a hemiplegia on the opposite side. It locates the lesion to a level in the brainstem, the cranial nerve involved indicating the level.

evidence.quote: A peripheral cranial nerve lesion on one side with a hemiplegia on the other locates the lesion to a level in the brainstem.
Alternating syndrome: ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy plus contralateral hemiplegia.

definitions.text: An ascending conscious tract running through the brainstem that carries crude touch, pain and temperature.

evidence.quote: Anterolateral (spinothalamic) | Ascending, conscious | Crude touch, pain, temperature
Conscious tracts : comprised of the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway and the anterolateral system.

definitions.text: Small paired laryngeal cartilage shaped like a triangular pyramid about 15 mm high. Its apex articulates with the corniculate cartilage and its concave base with the cricoid lamina; the base bears the vocal process anteriorly and the muscular process laterally.

evidence.quote: Triangular pyramids about 15 mm high. The apex articulates with the corniculate cartilage, the concave base with the cricoid lamina
The anterior angle of the base is extended by the vocal process

definitions.text: The artery lying in the basilar groove on the midline of the ventral surface of the pons. With its branches it gives the vascular supply of the brainstem.

evidence.quote: The basilar groove holds the basilar artery.
The brainstem receives vascular supply from the basilar artery and its branches.

definitions.text: The stalk connecting the cerebrum to the spinal cord and cerebellum, lying in the posterior cranial fossa on the clivus. It has three parts from above down (midbrain, pons, medulla), gives rise to ten of the twelve cranial nerves and runs vital functions.

evidence.quote: The brainstem connects the cerebrum to the spinal cord and cerebellum.
The brainstem is the structure that connects the cerebrum to the spinal cord and cerebellum.

title: Cadaveric position of the vocal cords
subject: subj:anat3

definitions.text: Position in which the vocal cords are further abducted and fixed because all the intrinsic muscles are paralysed, seen when both the recurrent and the external laryngeal nerves are damaged on both sides.

evidence.quote: If both recurrent and external laryngeal nerves are damaged on both sides, all the intrinsic muscles are paralysed and the cords are further abducted and fixed: the cadaveric position
This is known as the cadaveric postion of vocal cords

definitions.text: One of three paired peduncles (superior, middle and inferior) by which each part of the brainstem is connected to the cerebellum behind it. The peduncles also form part of the side walls of the fourth ventricle.

evidence.quote: Behind, the cerebellum by the cerebellar peduncles: superior to the midbrain, middle to the pons, inferior to the medulla.
Each part of brainstem is connected to cerebellum by cerebellar peduncles (superior, middle & inferior).

definitions.text: The angle at the junction of the pons, medulla and cerebellum, where the cerebellar flocculus, the choroid plexus and the emerging cranial nerves VII and VIII surround the foramen of Luschka, the lateral aperture of the fourth ventricle.

evidence.quote: The cerebellopontine angle, where CN VII and VIII emerge beside the foramen of Luschka, lies at the junction of pons, medulla and cerebellum.
The angle formed at the junction of the pons, medulla, and cerebellum is another anatomical landmark and is named cerebellopontine angle.

definitions.text: The part of the ependymal cavity of the brainstem that runs through the midbrain, with the tectum lying behind it.

evidence.quote: Aqueduct runs through the midbrain.
Tectum: located posterior to the cerebral aqueduct

definitions.text: One of the paired pillars on the anterolateral midbrain, running from the cerebral hemispheres to converge at the pons and carrying descending fibres. The two are separated anteriorly in the midline by the interpeduncular fossa.

evidence.quote: Cerebral peduncles, paired and anterolateral, separated by the interpeduncular fossa.
The paired cerebral peduncles extend from the cerebral hemispheres to converge as they meet the pons.

definitions.text: Small paired accessory cartilage of the larynx lying on the apex of the arytenoid cartilage, with which it articulates.

evidence.quote: Corniculate: on the apices of the arytenoids
Three paired and small: arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform

definitions.text: A descending motor tract which, with the corticobulbar tract, forms the motor pathway for voluntary movement of the body and face. It produces the pyramid of the medulla, and 75 to 90 percent of its fibres decussate in the lower medulla.

evidence.quote: Corticospinal and corticobulbar | Descending | Voluntary movement of body and face
Pyramids = corticospinal tracts; 75-90% decussate in the lower medulla.

definitions.text: Elliptical synovial joint uniting the base of the arytenoid with the upper edge of the cricoid lamina, reinforced by the posterior cricoarytenoid ligament. Functionally the most important laryngeal joint, allowing rotation of the arytenoid around a vertical axis and gliding of the arytenoids toward or away from each other.

evidence.quote: An elliptical synovial articulation reinforced by the posterior cricoarytenoid ligament, uniting the base of the arytenoid with the upper edge of the cricoid lamina
Rotatory movement, in which arytenoid cartilage moves around a vertical axis, thus abducting or adducting the vocal cords

definitions.text: Unpaired signet-shaped ring of cartilage with a narrow anterior arch and a broad posterior lamina, at the level of C6. It is the only cartilage that completely encircles the lumen of the larynx and is called the foundation stone of the larynx.

evidence.quote: A signet-shaped ring with a narrow anterior arch and a broad posterior lamina, at C6
The cricoid cartilage is situated at the level of C6 vertebra and completely encircles the lumen of the larynx

definitions.text: Flat synovial joint, reinforced by ligaments, joining the lower cornu of the thyroid cartilage and the lateral face of the cricoid cartilage. It allows tilting of the cricoid around a transverse axis, the arch up and the lamina down.

evidence.quote: A flat synovial joint reinforced by ligaments, joining the lower cornu of the thyroid cartilage and the lateral face of the cricoid
Flat synovial joint reinforced by ligaments joining the lower cornu of the thyroid cartilage and the lateral face of the cricoid cartilage

definitions.text: Intrinsic ligament of the larynx, part of the fibroelastic inner tube, described as stretched between the thyroid cartilage and the vocal process, where it forms the vocal ligament. With the cricoid it surrounds the infraglottic cavity.

evidence.quote: The cricothyroid ligament, stretched between the thyroid cartilage and the vocal process, forms the vocal ligament
The cavity below the vocal cords, surrounded by the cricoid and the cricothyroid ligament

definitions.text: Paired intrinsic muscle and the only one lying on the outer aspect of the larynx. It elevates the cricoid arch and lowers the thyroid cartilage, tensing the vocal cord, and is important for the tone and pitch of the voice.

evidence.quote: Vocal cord tensors: cricothyroid (paired). Action: elevation of the cricoid arch and lowering of the thyroid cartilage, tensing the vocal cord
Crivothyroid: tenses the vocal cords

definitions.text: Small paired accessory cartilage of the larynx lying in the aryepiglottic fold.

evidence.quote: Cuneiform: in the aryepiglottic fold
Three paired and small: arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform

definitions.text: An ascending conscious tract running through the brainstem that carries touch, proprioception and vibration.

evidence.quote: Dorsal column-medial lemniscus | Ascending, conscious | Touch, proprioception, vibration
Conscious tracts : comprised of the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway and the anterolateral system.

definitions.text: Large unpaired laryngeal cartilage shaped like a tennis racket. Its posterior (laryngeal) side faces the vestibule and its anterior (lingual) side the base of the tongue and hyoid; its base is superior and free and its foot inserts into the reentrant angle of the thyroid cartilage.

evidence.quote: Shaped like a tennis racket with a curved lower handle forming its foot
Shape: tennis racket with curved lower handle forming the foot of the epiglottis

aliases: external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve

definitions.text: Branch of the superior laryngeal nerve that innervates the cricothyroid muscle. The lecture also says it perforates the cricothyroid membrane and gives sensory innervation to the subglottic stage.

evidence.quote: External branch | Innervates the cricothyroid muscle and perforates the cricothyroid membrane; sensory innervation of the subglottic stage
External branch - innervates cricothyroid m

definitions.text: Lesion of the external laryngeal nerve that paralyses the cricothyroid muscle, giving weakness of phonation from loss of its tightening effect on the vocal cords. The voice change is especially noticeable in singers.

evidence.quote: External laryngeal nerve: weakness of phonation from loss of the tightening effect of the cricothyroid
Paralysis after an external laryngeal nerve lesion alters the voice significantly, especially noticeable in singers

definitions.text: Muscle ensuring laryngeal mobility, especially during swallowing. The elevators are the thyrohyoid, mylohyoid and digastric; the depressors are the sternothyroid, sternohyoid and omohyoid.

evidence.quote: Extrinsic muscles ensure laryngeal mobility, especially during swallowing. Elevators: thyrohyoid, mylohyoid, digastric. Depressors: sternothyroid, sternohyoid, omohyoid
Extrinsic muscles: ensure laryngeal mobility especially during swallowing

definitions.text: A bulge in the floor of the fourth ventricle, on the posterior surface of the pons, formed by the fibres of the facial nerve looping round the abducens nucleus.

evidence.quote: Facial colliculus: facial fibres looping around the abducens nucleus.
The facial colliculus is a bulging formed by the fibres of the facial nerve looping around the abducens nucleus.

definitions.text: Cranial nerve VII, which emerges at the cerebellopontine angle, the more lateral aspect of the pontomedullary junction, with the intermediate nerve of Wrisberg (VII bis) and the vestibulocochlear nerve lateral to it. Its fibres loop round the abducens nucleus.

evidence.quote: CN VII, facial | Cerebellopontine angle
Cranial nerve VII: facial originates from the cerebellopontine angle, the more lateral aspect of the pontomedullary junction.

definitions.text: The peak of the fourth ventricle, within the cerebellum, lying under the fastigial nucleus.

evidence.quote: The peak is the fastigium; the caudal tip the obex
The peak of the fourth ventricle within the cerebellum is the fastigium and it underlies the fastigial nucleus.

definitions.text: The ependymal cavity behind the pons and medulla. Its roof is the superior and inferior medullary vela, its floor the rhomboid fossa and its side walls the vela and cerebellar peduncles; CSF leaves by the median foramen of Magendie and two lateral foramina of Luschka.

evidence.quote: Roof: the superior and inferior medullary vela. Floor: the rhomboid fossa. Side walls: the vela and cerebellar peduncles.
CSF exits via Magendie (median) and Luschka (lateral)

definitions.text: Cranial nerve IX, one of the mixed nerves, which leaves the lateral surface of the medulla behind the olive, above the vagus.

evidence.quote: Lateral, behind the olive | IX, X and XI, the mixed nerves
Glossopharyngeal nerve (IX): leaves the medulla behind the olive, above the vagus.

definitions.text: The compartment of the larynx at the level of the two vocal cords, which delimit a triangular opening. It is narrower than the vestibular cleft.

evidence.quote: The glottis is triangular and narrower than the vestibular cleft
Glottis: delimited by the 2 vocal cords, it is triangular in shape

definitions.text: Bone lying above the larynx with the base of the tongue. The larynx is united to it through muscles and ligaments, and the thyrohyoid membrane reaches its lower edge.

evidence.quote: Above: the hyoid bone and base of the tongue
Top: hyoid bone and base of tongue

definitions.text: Cranial nerve XII, which emerges from the anterior surface of the medulla in the sulcus between the pyramid and the olive.

evidence.quote: CN XII emerges between pyramid and olive
Hypoglossal(12th): from sulcus between pyramid & olive

definitions.text: The cerebellar peduncle that connects the medulla oblongata with the cerebellum.

evidence.quote: Cerebellar peduncles: superior to midbrain, middle to pons, inferior to medulla.
Inferior peduncle connects medulla oblongata with cerebellum

definitions.text: One of the lower pair of rounded prominences of the tectum on the back of the midbrain. Its fibres, with those of the lateral lemniscus, run in the inferior brachium to the medial geniculate body (hearing).

evidence.quote: the inferior brachium carries lateral lemniscus and inferior colliculus fibres to the medial geniculate body (hearing)
The lower pair of bumps on the back of the midbrain: auditory pathway.

definitions.text: The nucleus of the medulla that produces the olive; it is important in the control of movement.

evidence.quote: Olive = inferior olivary nucleus.
Produced by inferior olivary nucleus (important in control of movement).

definitions.text: The cavity of the larynx below the vocal cords, surrounded by the cricoid cartilage and the cricothyroid ligament.

evidence.quote: The cavity below the vocal cords, surrounded by the cricoid and the cricothyroid ligament
Infraglottic cavity — space inferior to vocal folds

aliases: internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve

definitions.text: Branch of the superior laryngeal nerve that enters the larynx with the superior laryngeal artery by perforating the thyrohyoid membrane. It gives sensory innervation to the mucosa above the vocal folds, plus autonomic fibres.

evidence.quote: Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve: sensation above the cords, piercing the thyrohyoid membrane
Pierces thyrohyoid membrane + Sensory from mucosa above vocal folds

definitions.text: Muscle of the larynx classified by its action as a vocal cord tensor, dilator of the glottis or constrictor of the glottis. All are paired except the transverse arytenoid, and all are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve except the cricothyroid.

evidence.quote: All the intrinsic muscles are paired except the transverse arytenoid (interarytenoid), which is unpaired
Recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic muscles except the cricothyroid

definitions.text: Thin, smooth, pale pink lining of the larynx, continuous with the pharyngeal mucosa above and the tracheal mucosa below. Its epithelium is respiratory type (cylindric stratified) except at the vocal cords and upper half of the epiglottis, where it is non-keratinized stratified squamous.

evidence.quote: The epithelium is respiratory type (cylindric stratified) throughout, except at the vocal cords and the upper half of the epiglottis, which are non-keratinized stratified squamous
Thin, smooth, pale pink in color. It continues above with the pharyngeal mucosa and below with the tracheal mucosa

definitions.text: Blockage of the larynx by a foreign body, causing choking when the explosive cough reflex set off by the very sensitive mucosa of the superior larynx is slowed or absent. The Heimlich manoeuvre of upward and backward abdominal thrusts is used to dislodge the foreign body.

evidence.quote: The mucosa of the superior larynx is very sensitive, so a foreign body causes immediate explosive coughing. If that reflex is slowed or absent, choking follows
give three or four abdominal thrusts directed upwards and backwards, squeezing the residual air up to dislodge the foreign body

definitions.text: The forward bulge formed where the two laminae of the thyroid cartilage meet in the midline.

evidence.quote: The laryngeal prominence, the Adam's apple, formed where the two laminae of the thyroid cartilage meet in the midline
the forward bulge where the two thyroid laminae meet

definitions.text: Cavity of the supraglottic compartment of the larynx lying between the ventricular bands (false vocal cords, vestibular folds) above and the plane of the vocal cords below.

evidence.quote: Laryngeal or Morgagni ventricle: between the ventricular bands (false vocal cords) above and the plane of the vocal cords below
ventricle between them and the vocal folds

definitions.text: Pyramidal space of the supraglottic compartment of the larynx, extending from the laryngeal margin to the ventricular bands: the space above the vestibular folds.

evidence.quote: Vestibule: a pyramidal space from the laryngeal margin to the ventricular bands
vestibule above the vestibular folds

definitions.text: The upper expanded part of the lower respiratory tract, modified for producing voice: an unpaired median tube of cartilages linked by joints, muscles and ligaments and lined by mucous membrane. It acts as a sphincter at the inlet of the lower respiratory tract.

evidence.quote: The larynx is the upper expanded part of the lower respiratory tract, modified for producing voice, also called the organ of phonation
It acts as a sphincter at the inlet of lower respiratory tract to protect the trachea and the bronchial tree

definitions.text: Paired intrinsic muscle of the larynx inserting on the muscular process of the arytenoid; a constrictor of the glottis that adducts the vocal cords.

evidence.quote: the lateral angle bears the muscular process (insertion of the posterior and lateral cricoarytenoid muscles)
Lateral cricoarytenoids: adduct the vocal cords

definitions.text: Laryngeal lymphatics are very rich in the supraglottic zone, thinner in the subglottic zone and absent at the vocal cords. The supraglottic region drains to the internal jugular chain; the infraglottic region to pretracheal and paratracheal nodes and the internal jugular chain.

evidence.quote: Very rich in the supraglottic zone, thinner in the subglottic zone, absent at the vocal cords. Supraglottic: the internal jugular chain
Very rich in the supraglottic zones, thinner in the subglottic zone, absent in the vocal cords

definitions.text: The lowest part of the brainstem, continuous below with the spinal cord. Its ventral surface bears the pyramids and olives, and it houses the respiratory and cardiovascular centres.

evidence.quote: Medulla: pyramids (corticospinal), olives (inferior olivary nucleus)
the respiratory and cardiovascular centres are in the medulla

definitions.text: The third embryonic vesicle, which forms the midbrain.

evidence.quote: Midbrain | Mesencephalon (third vesicle)
the mesencephalon (third vesicle)

definitions.text: The fourth embryonic vesicle, which forms the pons together with the cerebellum.

evidence.quote: Pons | Metencephalon (fourth vesicle)
The largest part, from the metencephalon with the cerebellum.

definitions.text: The uppermost and smallest part of the brainstem, about 2 cm long, passing through the tentorial opening (foramen of Pacchioni). It has two parts: the tectum behind the cerebral aqueduct and the paired cerebral peduncles anterolaterally.

evidence.quote: Midbrain: smallest, 2 cm; tectum with four colliculi; peduncles with CN III between them.
The midbrain is the smallest of the three regions of the brainstem, measuring around 2cm in length.

definitions.text: The cerebellar peduncle that connects the pons with the cerebellum; the largest of the three.

evidence.quote: middle → pons (largest)
Middle peduncle connects pons with cerebellum

definitions.text: The fifth embryonic vesicle, which forms the medulla oblongata.

evidence.quote: Medulla oblongata | Myelencephalon (fifth vesicle)
the myelencephalon (fifth vesicle)

definitions.text: The most caudal tip of the fourth ventricle.

evidence.quote: obex at its caudal tip
The obex is the most caudal tip of the fourth ventricle.

definitions.text: Cranial nerve III, which emerges from the anterior surface of the midbrain between the two cerebral peduncles, in the interpeduncular fossa.

evidence.quote: Anterior, midbrain | III between the cerebral peduncles
The oculomotor nerve (CN III) is seen exiting from between the peduncles

definitions.text: Cranial nerve I; with the optic nerve, one of the two cranial nerves that do not arise from the brainstem.

evidence.quote: All cranial nerves arise from the brainstem except the optic and olfactory nerves.
All cranial nerves arise from the brainstem, with the exception of two: the optic nerve and the olfactory nerve.

definitions.text: An elevation on the medulla lying lateral to the pyramid, produced by the inferior olivary nucleus.

evidence.quote: the olive lateral to it by the inferior olivary nucleus
An elevation, lies lateral to the pyramid.

definitions.text: Cranial nerve II, running from the eye to the optic chiasm; with the olfactory nerve, one of the two cranial nerves that do not arise from the brainstem.

evidence.quote: All cranial nerves arise from the brainstem except the optic and olfactory nerves.
runs from the eye to the optic chiasm

definitions.text: The set of mechanisms allowing vibration at the free edge of the vocal fold, transforming aerodynamic energy into acoustic energy. The sound produced is then modified and filtered by the supralaryngeal air cavities to become vowels and consonants.

evidence.quote: The set of mechanisms allowing vibration at the free edge of the vocal fold, transforming aerodynamic energy into acoustic energy
The phonation (speech) is produced by the vibrations of the vocal cords

definitions.text: The middle and largest part of the brainstem. Its ventral bulge, about 2.5 cm, is made by transverse pontocerebellar fibres, and the basilar groove in its ventral midline holds the basilar artery.

evidence.quote: Its ventral bulge, about 2.5 cm, is made by transverse pontocerebellar fibres.
Pons: largest; basilar artery in the basilar groove; CN V to VIII.

definitions.text: The landmark defined by the angle between the lower border of the pons and the upper border of the medulla. Cranial nerves VI, VII and VIII emerge there from medial to lateral, and the fourth ventricle is widest at its level.

evidence.quote: VI, VII, VIII at the pontomedullary junction (medial to lateral)
The pontomedullary junction is an important anatomical landmark defined by the angle between the lower border of the pons and the superior border of the medulla.

definitions.text: The cranial fossa in which the brainstem lies, resting on the clivus under the tentorium cerebelli.

evidence.quote: It lies in the posterior cranial fossa, on the clivus, under the tentorium cerebelli
Brainstem: midbrain, pons, medulla, in the posterior cranial fossa on the clivus.

definitions.text: Paired intrinsic muscle of the larynx inserting on the muscular process of the arytenoid. It is the only dilator of the glottis and the only intrinsic muscle that abducts the vocal cords, hence called the safety muscle of the larynx.

evidence.quote: Posterior cricoarytenoids are the only abductors: the safety muscles of the larynx
Posterior ericoarytenoids: abduct the vocal cords

definitions.text: Branch of the inferior thyroid artery that supplies the posterior part of the laryngeal mucosa and anastomoses with the superior laryngeal artery.

evidence.quote: Posteroinferior laryngeal artery | A branch of the inferior thyroid artery. Supplies the posterior part of the laryngeal mucosa
branch of the Inferior Thyroid Artery. It vascularizes the posterior part of the laryngeal mucosa

definitions.text: An elevation on either side of the ventral median fissure of the medulla, produced by the corticospinal tract.

evidence.quote: The pyramid on each side is made by the corticospinal tract
Produced by corticospinal tract.

definitions.text: The crossing of most corticospinal (pyramidal) fibres, 75 to 90 percent, in the lower medulla; it marks the lower part of the ventral median fissure.

evidence.quote: is marked below by the decussation of 75 to 90 percent of corticospinal fibres
Its lower part is marked by decussation of most of pyramidal(corticospinal) fibers (75%-90%).

definitions.text: Branch of the vagus arising on the right at the base of the neck and on the left in the thorax. It is motor to all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid and sensory below the vocal folds.

evidence.quote: From the vagus, on the right at the base of the neck and on the left at the thorax. Motor to all the intrinsic muscles except the cricothyroid
Recurrent laryngeal n. + Motor to intrinsic muscles of larynx

definitions.text: Damage to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, often accidental during partial thyroidectomy. Unilaterally, the cord on the affected side lies in the paramedian position and does not vibrate, though the other usually compensates; bilaterally, both cords lie paramedian with loss of phonation and difficulty breathing.

evidence.quote: Recurrent laryngeal nerve, often damaged accidentally during partial thyroidectomy: unilaterally, the cord lies in the paramedian position and does not vibrate, though the other usually compensates
Unilateral recurrent nerve palsy: paramedian cord

definitions.text: A network of neuronal cell bodies and small axon bundles running in many directions, without distinct boundaries, spread from the spinal cord through the brainstem to the hypothalamus and thalamus. It integrates arousal, consciousness, sleep-wake cycles, motor coordination, cardiovascular and respiratory control and pain modulation.

evidence.quote: It integrates vital functions: arousal, consciousness, sleep-wake cycles, motor coordination, cardiovascular and respiratory control, pain modulation and habituation.
The reticular formation (RF) consists of an intricate mixture of neuronal cell bodies and fascicles of axons running in small bundles

definitions.text: The diamond-shaped depression on the dorsal surface of the pons and the upper half of the medulla that forms the floor of the fourth ventricle.

evidence.quote: fourth ventricle floor is the rhomboid fossa
The floor, located ventrally, is formed by the rhomboid fossa, a diamond-shaped depression on the dorsal surface of the pons and upper half of the medulla.

title: Stria medullaris of the fourth ventricle
subject: subj:anat3

definitions.text: A bundle of nerve fibres crossing the floor of the fourth ventricle transversely from the lateral aspect into the midline. It marks the posterior border between the pons and the medulla.

evidence.quote: the stria medullaris marking the pons-medulla border
The stria medullaris of the fourth ventricle is a bundle of nerve fibres crossing transversely from the lateral aspect into the midline.

definitions.text: The cerebellar peduncle that connects the midbrain with the cerebellum.

evidence.quote: Cerebellar peduncles: superior to midbrain, middle to pons, inferior to medulla.
Superior peduncle connects midbrain with cerebellum

definitions.text: One of the upper pair of rounded prominences of the tectum on the back of the midbrain, linked with the retina by the superior brachium and concerned with vision.

evidence.quote: The superior brachium links the superior colliculus with the retina (vision)
The upper pair of bumps on the back of the midbrain: visual reflexes.

definitions.text: Branch of the superior thyroid artery that enters the larynx through the thyrohyoid membrane with the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. It supplies the supraglottic part and anastomoses with the posteroinferior laryngeal artery.

evidence.quote: Superior laryngeal artery | A branch of the superior thyroid artery. Supplies the supraglottic part and anastomoses with the posteroinferior laryngeal artery
branch of the Superior Thyroid Artery, it vascularizes the supraglottic part and anastomoses with ALPI

definitions.text: Branch of the vagus, mixed but essentially sensory, that descends against the pharyngeal wall and divides behind the greater horn of the hyoid into an internal and an external branch.

evidence.quote: A branch of the vagus, mixed but essentially sensory, descending against the pharyngeal wall and dividing behind the greater horn of the hyoid

definitions.text: A band extending laterally from the superior colliculus that forms a pathway between the superior colliculus and the retina of the eye, serving vision.

evidence.quote: The superior brachium links the superior colliculus with the retina (vision)
Superior quadrigeminal brachium forms a pathway between the superior colliculus and the retina of the eye( vision).

definitions.text: One of the air cavities above the larynx, chiefly the pharynx and the oral cavity, which filter the laryngeal sound by resonance and shape it by articulation through the tongue, pharyngolarynx, jaws, lips and soft palate.

evidence.quote: The sound produced is immediately modified and filtered by the supralaryngeal air cavities to become vowels and consonants
Filter role: resonance and enrichment of certain frequencies or suppression of others, with two areas of particular enhancement, the pharynx and the oral cavity

definitions.text: The part of the midbrain behind the cerebral aqueduct. It houses four rounded colliculi, two superior and two inferior, just below the pineal gland.

evidence.quote: Tectum, behind the cerebral aqueduct: two superior and two inferior colliculi below the pineal gland.
The tectum houses four rounded prominences named colliculi which sit directly inferior to the pineal gland.

definitions.text: A structure belonging to the diencephalon; it is not part of the brainstem.

evidence.quote: The thalamus is NOT brainstem.
The thalamus belongs to the diencephalon.

definitions.text: Intrinsic muscle of the larynx that relaxes the vocal cords. The lecture lists a superior part, from the reentrant angle of the thyroid cartilage to the lower third of the arytenoid, and an inferior part among the constrictors of the glottis.

evidence.quote: Relax the vocal cords | Thyroarytenoid
Thyroarytenoid: relaxes the vocal cords

definitions.text: Extrinsic ligament of the larynx attaching the lower narrow end (foot) of the epiglottis to the posterior surface of the thyroid angle.

evidence.quote: Thyroepiglottic ligament: attaches the lower narrow end of the epiglottis to the posterior surface of the thyroid angle
inferior inserts into the reentrant angle of the thyroid cartilage through the thyroepiglottic ligament

definitions.text: Extrinsic membrane of the larynx running from the upper edge of the thyroid cartilage to the lower edge of the hyoid bone, with a medial and two lateral thickenings. The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve and the superior laryngeal artery perforate it.

evidence.quote: Thyrohyoid membrane: from the upper edge of the thyroid cartilage to the lower edge of the hyoid bone
Enters the larynx with the superior laryngeal artery by perforating the thyrohyoid membrane

definitions.text: Large unpaired laryngeal cartilage shaped like an open book, open backwards, with two vertical quadrilateral laminae, superior and inferior thyroid incisures and superior and inferior cornua; the inferior cornu carries a cricoid articular surface.

evidence.quote: Shaped like an open book, open backwards, with two vertical quadrilateral laminae
a thick vertical posterior margin extended by the superior and inferior cornua, the inferior carrying a cricoid articular surface

definitions.text: The airway lying below the larynx, with which the larynx is continuous. The cricotracheal ligament runs between the lower edge of the cricoid and the upper edge of the first tracheal ring.

evidence.quote: Above: the hyoid bone and base of the tongue. Below: the trachea
Cricotracheal ligament: between the lower edge of the cricoid and the upper edge of the first tracheal ring

definitions.text: The only unpaired intrinsic muscle of the larynx, inserting on the posterior side of the arytenoid cartilages; a constrictor of the glottis that adducts the vocal cords.

evidence.quote: All the intrinsic muscles are paired except the transverse arytenoid (interarytenoid), which is unpaired
Posterior side: gives insertion to the transverse arytenoid muscle

definitions.text: The fissure at the upper limit of the brainstem, by which the brainstem connects above with the diencephalon.

evidence.quote: Above, the diencephalon by the transverse fissure of Bichat.
Above: diencephalon by transverse fissure of BICHAT

definitions.text: Cranial nerve V, a large nerve that emerges from the lateral aspect of the mid-pons.

evidence.quote: CN V, trigeminal | Lateral mid-pons
Cranial nerve V: trigeminal originates from the lateral aspect of mid pons

definitions.text: Cranial nerve IV, which emerges from the dorsal surface of the midbrain below the inferior colliculi before sweeping round to the anterior surface. It is the only cranial nerve that emerges dorsally.

evidence.quote: Posterior, midbrain | IV, the only nerve emerging dorsally
Inferior to the colliculi, the trochlear nerve (CN IV) emerges before sweeping across to the anterior surface.

definitions.text: Cranial nerve X, one of the mixed nerves, which leaves the lateral surface of the medulla behind the olive, below the glossopharyngeal nerve.

evidence.quote: Lateral, behind the olive | IX, X and XI, the mixed nerves
Vagus nerve (X): leaves the medulla behind the olive, below IX.

definitions.text: Cranial nerve VIII, which emerges lateral to the facial nerve at the cerebellopontine angle.

evidence.quote: CN VIII, vestibulocochlear | Lateral to CN VII
Cranial nerve VIII: vestibulocochlear originates laterally to the facial nerve.

definitions.text: The cycle of vocal fold movement during phonation: the folds close as the arytenoids come together; they open when subglottic pressure overcomes the muscular and elastic resistance, letting a puff of air pass at high speed; then the folds close again.

evidence.quote: Putting into phonatory position: the folds close as the arytenoids come together
Opening: when the subglottic pressure overcomes the muscular and elastic resistance, a puff of air passes at high speed, an acoustic impulse

definitions.text: One of two pearly white cords stretched between the reentrant angle of the thyroid cartilage in front and the arytenoid cartilage behind, made of vocal ligament and muscle. The two unite anteriorly at the anterior commissure and are separated posteriorly by the interarytenoid region.

evidence.quote: Two pearly white vocal cords stretched between the reentrant angle of the thyroid cartilage in front and the arytenoid behind, made of vocal ligament and muscle
2 pearly white cords stretched between the reentrant angle of the thyroid cartilage in front and the arytenoid cartilage in back

definitions.text: Movement in which the arytenoids rotate so that their vocal processes move laterally, giving a wide diamond-shaped opening of the glottis that lets air through the rima glottidis.

evidence.quote: the muscular processes of both arytenoids rotate medially and the vocal processes rotate laterally, giving a wide diamond-shaped opening
moves around a vertical axis, thus abducting or adducting the vocal cords

definitions.text: Movement bringing the vocal cords together, produced by rotation of the arytenoids around a vertical axis at the cricoarytenoid joint. Keeping the cords adducted is the first step of voice production.

evidence.quote: Rotatory movement around a vertical axis, abducting or adducting the vocal cords
The voice is produced in following manner: 1. Vocal cords are kept adducted

definitions.text: Tightening of the vocal cord that makes it ready to vibrate when sound is about to be produced; it is produced by tilting of the cricoid around a transverse axis at the cricothyroid joint.

evidence.quote: Tilting of the cricoid around a transverse axis (arch up, lamina down) tenses the vocal cords
when sound is about to be produced it tenses the cord and makes it ready to vibrate

definitions.text: Ligament formed by the cricothyroid ligament between the thyroid cartilage and the vocal process of the arytenoid, on which it inserts. Together with muscle it makes up the vocal cord.

evidence.quote: The cricothyroid ligament, stretched between the thyroid cartilage and the vocal process, forms the vocal ligament
The vocal process gives insertion to the : • Vocal ligament

definitions.text: Inflammatory nodule that develops in people who overuse the voice, at the junction of the anterior one third and posterior two thirds of the vocal cords, the area of maximum contact during vibration. Nodules are bilateral and symmetrical, soft and reddish early, later greyish or whitish.

evidence.quote: Vocal nodules form at the junction of the anterior third and posterior two thirds of the cords
teachers, pop singers, the inflammatory nodules develop at these sites called vocal nodules

definitions.text: The extension of the anterior angle of the base of the arytenoid cartilage, which gives insertion to the vocal ligament.

evidence.quote: The anterior angle of the base extends as the vocal process (insertion of the vocal ligament)
The vocal process gives insertion to the : • Vocal ligament

definitions.text: Intrinsic muscle of the larynx, named in the lecture as the inferior thyroarytenoid, running from the reentrant angle of the thyroid cartilage to the anterolateral aspect of the arytenoid. It tilts the arytenoid forward and tenses the vocal cord.

evidence.quote: inferior thyroarytenoid or vocal muscle (from the reentrant angle to the anterolateral aspect of the arytenoid), which tilts the arytenoid forward and tenses the cord
Vocals: tenses the vocal cords
